meta.description: Flags hedges that carry no information about actual uncertainty.

examples.bad: It might be said that the contract is, in some sense, ambiguous.
examples.good: The contract is ambiguous because clause 4 conflicts with clause 9.

meta.rationale: A hedge earns its place only when it tells the reader what is uncertain and why. Stacked qualifiers with no stated reason are AI filler.

meta.description: Flags achievement language and hype in reports, PRs, and docs.

examples.bad: Successfully implemented comprehensive error handling to ensure reliable performance.
examples.good: Added error handling to every API endpoint.

meta.rationale: Prose should state what changed and why. Words like “successfully”, “comprehensive”, and “flawless” praise the work instead of describing it, and are the tell of AI-written status updates. Say what happened; let the reader judge it.

meta.description: Flags “actually” when it adds emphasis instead of a fact.

examples.bad: The claim is actually weak.
examples.good: The claim is weak.

meta.rationale: Use “actually” only when it marks a legally relevant fact or correction.

meta.description: Flags common AI-writing clichés.

examples.bad: We should delve into this issue.
examples.good: We should examine this issue.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags links tagged with an AI assistant's utm_source referral parameter.

examples.bad: See https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78j?utm_source=chatgpt.com.
examples.good: See https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78j.

meta.rationale: ChatGPT tags the links it formats with utm_source=chatgpt.com. The tag is invisible in rendered text but shows on hover, and tells the reader the link came from ChatGPT.

meta.description: Flags repeated sentence openers across a document

examples.bad: The court reviewed the motion and the supporting record. The court considered the response from both parties. The court examined the affidavits submitted with the motion. The court compared those affidavits with the hearing transcript. The court rejected the unsupported account. The court denied relief on the present record. The court entered judgment for the respondent. The court retained jurisdiction over costs.
examples.good: The court reviewed the motion and the supporting record. It considered the response from both parties, compared the affidavits with the hearing transcript, and rejected the unsupported account. Relief was denied on the present record, and the court retained jurisdiction over costs.

meta.description: Flags rhetorical antithesis that balances one idea against another.

examples.bad: It is not the tool, but the workflow, that determines the result.
examples.good: The workflow determines the result.

meta.rationale: Balanced opposition can make prose sound staged when it replaces a direct statement with a memorable contrast.

meta.description: Flags formulaic binary-contrast constructions.

examples.bad: The question isn't the model. It's the eval.
examples.good: The eval matters more than the model.

meta.rationale: State the substantive point directly instead of staging a false choice.

meta.description: Flags dramatic colon reveals at sentence starts.

examples.bad: The best part: it learns from mistakes.
examples.good: It learns from mistakes.

meta.rationale: Use colons for lists, labels, and quotes, not staged revelations.

meta.description: Flags formulaic contrasting pairs

examples.bad: The analysis should be clear without becoming simplistic, balanced without becoming vague.
examples.good: The analysis should be clear and balanced.

meta.rationale: State the quality or limitation directly instead of balancing paired opposites.

meta.description: Flags corporate-register verbs

examples.bad: The report showcases the team's capabilities.
examples.good: The report shows what the team can do.

meta.rationale: Prefer concrete verbs over corporate language that inflates ordinary actions.

meta.description: Flags corrective-negation constructions

examples.bad: It's not that the rule is unclear, it's that the record is incomplete.
examples.good: The record is incomplete.

meta.rationale: State the substantive point without staging a correction.

meta.description: Flags worn-out metaphors and figures of speech.

examples.bad: The settlement was low-hanging fruit for the plaintiff.
examples.good: The plaintiff settled the claim quickly and cheaply.

meta.rationale: Orwell's first rule: never use a figure of speech you are used to seeing in print. A dead metaphor no longer calls up an image; it just fills space. State the point plainly.

meta.description: Flags legal doublets and triplets

examples.bad: The contract is null and void.
examples.good: The contract is void.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags dramatic fragments and negative-listing constructions.

examples.bad: Not a bug. Not a feature. A policy choice.
examples.good: This is a policy choice.

meta.rationale: Use complete sentences and state the conclusion without staged fragments.

meta.description: Flags excessive em dashes

examples.bad: The court—wisely—paused.
examples.good: The court wisely paused.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags em dashes

examples.bad: The court—wisely—paused.
examples.good: The court wisely paused.

meta.rationale: Use commas, parentheses, or a new sentence instead of an em dash.

meta.description: Flags overused empty emphasis words

examples.bad: This is very significantly important.
examples.good: This raises damages by forty percent.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags en dashes outside numeric ranges.

examples.bad: The court–ordered remedy failed.
examples.good: The range spans 2020–2024.

meta.rationale: En dashes belong only in numeric ranges such as 2020–2024. Elsewhere they read as stray punctuation.

meta.description: Flags faux-insight setups that posture before making a claim.

examples.bad: The part everyone misses: distribution is the real moat.
examples.good: Distribution is the moat.

meta.rationale: Make the claim stand on its own instead of flattering the writer as the lone expert.

meta.description: Flags filler intensifiers

examples.bad: The result is genuinely important.
examples.good: The result is important.

meta.rationale: Remove intensifiers that add emphasis without adding evidence.

meta.description: Flags decorative foreign phrases with an everyday English equivalent.

examples.bad: The clause covers, inter alia, indemnity and, vis-à-vis the guarantor, notice.
examples.good: The clause covers indemnity and, for the guarantor, notice, among other things.

meta.rationale: Orwell's fifth rule: never use a foreign phrase if you can think of an everyday English equivalent. This targets ornamental Latin, not legal terms of art (res judicata, prima facie, habeas corpus, mens rea, stare decisis, de novo), which have no plain substitute.

meta.description: Flags excessive hedging language

examples.bad: Perhaps the claim is arguably strong.
examples.good: The claim is strong.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags inflated claims about importance or status.

examples.bad: The launch marks a pivotal moment for the company.
examples.good: The launch is the company's first paid product.

meta.rationale: State the fact and let the reader judge whether it matters.

meta.description: Flags short closing sentences written for rhetorical effect.

examples.bad: The record contains no evidence of delivery. That's the whole game.
examples.good: The record contains no evidence of delivery. The notice was therefore ineffective.

meta.rationale: A punchy closer can perform finality without stating a holding or consequence.

meta.description: Flags archaic or unnecessarily formal legalese.

examples.bad: Pursuant to the agreement, the fee is due.
examples.good: Under the agreement, the fee is due.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags marketing language, hype, and filler.

examples.bad: We leverage a robust platform.
examples.good: We rely on a dependable platform.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags predictable sentence-length cadence

examples.bad: The court reviewed the record. The parties filed their briefs today. The clerk entered the order after the hearing. Counsel must comply with the judgment. The court considered each disputed fact in the record. The parties may renew the motion after discovery. The clerk shall serve the order on counsel. Counsel shall comply with the order.
examples.good: The court reviewed the motion. After extensive briefing, the record, including three depositions and two expert reports, still contains disputed facts that cannot be resolved on paper. Summary judgment is denied.

meta.description: Flags repeated negative parallelism

examples.bad: No delay. No explanation. No remedy.
examples.good: The record shows no delay, explanation, or remedy.

meta.rationale: Use a direct statement instead of a chain of negative fragments.

meta.description: Flags weak verbs paired with nominalized nouns

examples.bad: The court made a determination about the claim.
examples.good: The court determined the claim.

meta.rationale: Use the plain verb when it makes the sentence shorter and clearer.

meta.description: Flags not-only/but-also constructions

examples.bad: The ruling was not only wrong but also harmful.
examples.good: The ruling was wrong and harmful.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags excessive paired phrasing

examples.bad: The court sought clear and consistent rules for the parties. The parties offered careful and measured arguments about the record. The order should be fair and practical for everyone involved. The briefing presented precise and detailed objections to the proposed remedy. The witnesses gave calm and credible accounts during the hearing.
examples.good: The court sought clear rules for the parties. The parties offered measured arguments about the record. The order should work in practice. The briefing presented detailed objections to the proposed remedy. The witnesses gave credible accounts during the hearing.

meta.description: Flags paragraphs that open and close by repeating the same theme.

examples.bad: The record raises a notice problem. The parties exchanged several letters, but none stated the contractual deadline. The notice problem therefore remains the notice problem.
examples.good: The record raises a notice problem. The parties exchanged several letters, but none stated the contractual deadline. The court should therefore construe the notice provision against the drafter.

meta.rationale: Returning to the opening phrase as a closing beat pins the paragraph instead of moving the analysis forward.

meta.description: Flags repeated syntactic templates across sentences in a paragraph.

examples.bad: The court reviewed the motion. The court considered the response. The court rejected the argument.
examples.good: After reviewing the motion and response, the court rejected the argument.

meta.rationale: Repeated sentence templates can make a paragraph sound metronomic even when its words change.

meta.description: Flags marches of short coordinate clauses and sentences.

examples.bad: The court read the contract. It reviewed the emails. It considered the testimony. It denied the motion.
examples.good: After reviewing the contract, emails, and testimony, the court denied the motion.

meta.rationale: A string of equal short clauses can create a mechanical rhythm when the relationships between ideas deserve subordination.

meta.description: Flags frequent parenthetical asides

examples.bad: The court (again) delayed (twice).
examples.good: The court delayed again, twice.

examples.bad: The remedy (which the court ordered) failed.
examples.good: Under Section 4(b), the court-ordered remedy failed.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags likely passive-voice overuse

examples.bad: The motion was denied by the court.
examples.good: The court denied the motion.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags performed enthusiasm

examples.bad: We are thrilled to announce the new filing system.
examples.good: The new filing system is available.

meta.rationale: Use a factual description instead of performed affect.

meta.description: Flags repeated sentence openings.

examples.bad: The court erred. The record shows this plainly. The remedy is reversal.
examples.good: The court erred. Its record shows this plainly. Reversal is the remedy.

meta.description: Flags rhetorical setups that delay the substantive point.

examples.bad: What if I told you the filing deadline already passed?
examples.good: The filing deadline already passed.

meta.rationale: Make the point directly instead of staging a reveal for the reader.

meta.description: Flags overuse of formulaic transitions

examples.bad: Moreover, the claim fails.
examples.good: The claim also fails.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags dense repeated triplet constructions

examples.bad: The rule is clear, simple, and fair. The test is direct, narrow, and workable. The remedy is prompt, complete, and final. The record is old, incomplete, and unreliable. The briefing is careful, detailed, and extensive. The result is stable, predictable, and fair. The order is coherent, practical, and durable.
examples.good: The rule is clear and fair.

meta.rationale: Use this signal as a prompt to revise rhythm and density, not as a hard prohibition.

meta.description: Flags semicolons.

examples.bad: The motion failed; the court adjourned.
examples.good: The motion failed. The court adjourned.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags staged questions or tensions resolved by the next sentence.

examples.bad: What does the record show? It shows that the notice was late.
examples.good: The record shows that the notice was late.

meta.rationale: A setup followed by a manufactured payoff delays a direct point for dramatic effect.

meta.description: Flags stacked noun phrases before abstract head nouns

examples.bad: The agency adopted a long-term claims processing framework.
examples.good: The agency adopted a framework for processing claims over the long term.

meta.rationale: Unpack dense noun stacks so the relationship between ideas is explicit.

meta.description: Flags closing sentences that recap a paragraph without adding information.

examples.bad: The notice omitted the required date, so the agency could not verify when the appeal period began. The upshot is simple.
examples.good: The notice omitted the required date, so the agency could not verify when the appeal period began. The appeal was therefore timely.

meta.rationale: A summary beat announces the paragraph's point after the analysis is complete instead of carrying the analysis forward.

meta.description: Flags trailing participial clauses that pretend to explain significance.

examples.bad: The launch adds file search, highlighting the team's commitment to better workflows.
examples.good: The launch adds file search, so users can find old drafts without leaving the editor.

meta.rationale: Replace vague analysis with the concrete consequence or reason.

meta.description: Flags sycophantic openers

examples.bad: Great question. The statute controls.
examples.good: The statute controls.

meta.rationale: Start with the substance. Openers that add no information should be cut.

meta.description: Flags throat-clearing openers

examples.bad: Let me think about this. The claim fails.
examples.good: The claim fails.

meta.rationale: Start with the substance. Openers that add no information should be cut.

meta.description: Flags vague attributions without a named source.

examples.bad: Experts agree that the policy will fail.
examples.good: The 2024 Treasury report predicts the policy will fail.

meta.rationale: Name the source or cut the unsupported claim.

meta.description: Flags lists that omit the Oxford comma.

examples.bad: The parties are Alice, Bob and Carol.
examples.good: The parties are Alice, Bob, and Carol.

meta.rationale: Avoid patterns that can make otherwise clear prose sound formulaic or overworked.

meta.description: Flags sentences that restate the previous point without adding new information.

examples.bad: The statute of limitations has expired. In other words, the deadline for filing has passed.
examples.good: The statute of limitations has expired. The plaintiff filed on March 3, sixty days late.

meta.rationale: Restating a point in different words pads the text without informing the reader. Every sentence should add a fact, reason, example, or consequence.

meta.description: Flags padded phrases that a shorter word or nothing replaces.

examples.bad: Due to the fact that the deadline passed, we filed in order to preserve the claim.
examples.good: Because the deadline passed, we filed to preserve the claim.

meta.rationale: Orwell's third rule: if it is possible to cut a word out, cut it out. These stock phrases carry no more meaning than the single word that replaces them.

meta.description: Flags long words that have a short everyday equivalent.

examples.bad: The parties will utilize the platform to facilitate discovery.
examples.good: The parties will use the platform to help discovery.

meta.rationale: Orwell's second rule: never use a long word where a short one will do. Swap the long word only where the plain word carries the same meaning; keep terms of art.

meta.description: Flags prose that works on the page but not in a spoken explanation.

examples.bad: The foregoing analysis is dispositive with respect to the aforementioned issue in light of the fact that the parties' respective positions are mutually inconsistent.
examples.good: That analysis resolves the issue because the parties take conflicting positions.

meta.rationale: Clear legal writing can remain precise while using sentences a reader could say aloud.

meta.description: Flags sentences that are difficult to read.

examples.bad: The court, having reviewed the parties' extensive submissions and the voluminous record developed over three years of contentious litigation, and having heard four hours of oral argument on the competing motions for summary judgment, concludes that genuine disputes of material fact preclude judgment for either side at this stage of the proceedings.
examples.good: The court reviewed the record. Fact disputes preclude summary judgment.

meta.description: Flags documents dense with three-part parallel constructions.

examples.bad: The policy is clear, consistent, and fair. It protects employees, customers, and shareholders alike. Compliance requires training, monitoring, and enforcement. Each department must document, review, and certify its procedures. The board will assess progress quarterly, annually, and at each milestone. Managers must plan, supervise, and report their work. Auditors will test controls, trace transactions, and record exceptions. Counsel should identify risks, explain options, and recommend a course. The final report must be accurate, complete, and useful. The committee will review findings, assign owners, and track completion.
examples.good: The policy is clear and fair. It protects employees and customers, and compliance requires training backed by real enforcement. Each department documents its procedures; the board assesses progress quarterly.

meta.rationale: One rule-of-three is rhetoric; a document-wide habit of triads is machine cadence. Unlike the per-span core/no-rule-of-three density rule, this measures the whole document's rate.

meta.description: Flags documents whose sentence lengths barely vary.

examples.bad: The court reviewed the motion for summary judgment. The parties submitted their briefs on the scheduled date. The record contains several disputed factual questions. The governing standard requires viewing facts in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party. The court finds that genuine disputes preclude judgment here. The motion is therefore denied without prejudice to renewal. The clerk shall enter the order. Counsel shall comply with it.
examples.good: The court reviewed the motion. Both parties briefed it extensively, and the record, including three depositions, two expert reports, and a chain of emails read in incompatible ways, leaves genuine disputes of material fact. Summary judgment is denied.

meta.rationale: Human legal prose is bursty — long reasoning sentences sit next to short holdings and citations. Machine prose keeps sentence length uniform, and uniformity is much harder to prompt away than any word list.

meta.description: Flags modal verbs that can make technical instructions uncertain.

examples.bad: The service should restart after the update, and the request might fail.
examples.good: The service must restart after the update, and the request can fail.

meta.rationale: Use can, will, and must for clear possibility, prediction, and requirement. Replace other modals only when the intended meaning supports it.

meta.description: Flags words used with meanings or parts of speech that can confuse readers.

examples.bad: Check that the value is above 10 and follow the instructions.
examples.good: Make sure that the value is more than 10 and obey the instructions.

meta.rationale: Use one clear meaning for each common word. These checks cover frequent technical-writing substitutions, not the complete STE dictionary.

meta.description: Flags sentence-initial “this” without a following noun.

examples.bad: This shows that the cache is stale.
examples.good: This result shows that the cache is stale.

meta.rationale: A noun after “this” gives the reader a clear referent and reduces ambiguity.

meta.description: Flags instructions that put a required condition after the command.
Flags rotation between different words for the same concept.
Flags instructions written as descriptions or indirect suggestions.
Flags contractions that omit words in technical prose.

examples.bad: You can't restart it when it's locked.
examples.good: You cannot restart it when it is locked.

meta.rationale: Complete words reduce ambiguity for readers who do not speak English as a first language.

meta.description: Flags Latin abbreviations that can confuse technical readers.

examples.bad: Use a cache, e.g. Redis, i.e. a fast key-value store, etc.
examples.good: Use a cache, for example Redis, that is, a fast key-value store.

meta.rationale: Use plain English in place of Latin abbreviations, and name a complete list instead of using “etc.”

meta.description: Flags common phrasal verbs with clearer single-word alternatives.

examples.bad: Set up the service, then shut down the old process.
examples.good: Configure the service, then stop the old process.

meta.rationale: Single-word verbs are easier to translate and less likely to have several meanings. Choose the replacement that fits the context.

meta.description: Flags procedural sentences that contain more than one instruction.
Flags common inflated or vague words and phrases.

examples.bad: The robust service seamlessly enables you to leverage the functionality out of the box.
examples.good: The service lets you use the feature by default.

meta.rationale: Plain words improve translation and make technical facts easier to understand. Keep a technical term when it carries a precise domain meaning.

meta.description: Flags safety warnings that bury the command or condition after the risk.
Flags descriptive sentences longer than 25 words.

examples.bad: The service stores each request in the audit log and sends a response after it validates the token, checks the account, and applies the configured access policy.
examples.good: The service validates the token and stores the request in the audit log.

meta.rationale: STE Rule 6.3 sets a 25-word descriptive limit. Procedural text has a 20-word limit under Rule 5.1, but the engine cannot classify passages as procedural or descriptive. Quoted code, identifiers, numbers, titles, and text in parentheses count as one word under Rules 8.5-8.7.

meta.description: Flags complex verb constructions outside the simple tenses.

examples.bad: The migration has completed and the table is being rebuilt.
examples.good: The migration is complete. The system rebuilds the table.

meta.rationale: Simple verb forms reduce ambiguity for technical readers. This conservative check targets explicit auxiliary patterns and avoids guessing at every past participle.

meta.description: Flags technical nouns used as verbs when a direct construction is clearer.
